sources.title: Kim Jeong-hui (Q626484), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-24): English label 'Kim Jeong-hui', description 'Korean scholar, calligrapher (1786-1856)', Korean label 김정희, instance of human, born 1786, died 1856, citizen of Joseon. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.
Wikipedia, 'Kim Chŏnghŭi' (raw text read for orientation on dates, offices, the two exiles and the posthumous publication of his collected works). Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Encyclopedia of Korean Culture (Academy of Korean Studies), 'Kim Jeong-hui' (김정희), entry written in 2024 by Ryu Seung-min, a cultural-heritage appraisal committee member (read in full, in Korean). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: calls him the scholar-official, scholar and calligrapher-painter who founded the Joseon epigraphy school and completed the Chusa style; taught by Pak Je-ga, met Weng Fanggang, Ruan Yuan and other Qing scholars in Beijing in 1809, and renewed Joseon epigraphy; exiled to Jeju in 1840 for nine years in confinement, then to Bukcheong in 1851, and died in 1856; his scholarship rested on epigraphy and on classical studies (the 'Silsa gusi seol'), he studied Buddhism and argued with Seon masters while remaining their companion; he studied clerical script from Eastern Han stele rubbings and from bronze mirrors, lamps and bricks of the Western Han; the Jeju-era Chusa style broke popular taste, he called its strangeness 'goe' and wrote on an orchid painting that people would not understand or like it; he wrote the Chinese-style inscription 'Chimgye' only after looking for the right character for over thirty years; his masterpiece Sehando was painted in 1844 for the interpreter Yi Sang-jeok; he formed a circle that included Yi Ha-eung, Gwon Don-in, Jo Hui-ryong, Heo Ryeon and Jeon Gi. Expert reference entry from a national research institute, admiring but specific.

Encyclopedia of Korean Culture (Academy of Korean Studies), 'Geumseok gwaanrok' (금석과안록, the Silla Jinheung-wang monument study), entry by Jo Dong-won of Sungkyunkwan University (read in full, in Korean): his handwritten study of the Hwangchoryeong and Bukhansan monuments, which substantially revises the views set out in his earlier 'Jinheung-wang ibi go' through detailed checks: it matches the inscribed date with the Zhou calendar, uses the Samguk sakki and the Tang histories on titles, reads personal names and offices, picks the correct spelling of 'Chobang' from a collector's record, and dates the Bukhansan monument between 568 and 576, with letters to friends added. Specialist reference entry on a single work; it describes method, not personality.

The Korea Times (Kang Hyun-kyung), 'Joseon prodigy indulging in intellectual stimulation' (4 May 2018), report on art historian Yoo Hong-joon's biography 'Chusa Kim Jeong-hui: The Mountains Are High, The Seas Are Deep' (read in full): Kim as an epigrapher who identified the Jinheung monument on Mount Bukhan, who brought evidential scholarship home from the 1809 Beijing visit and corresponded with Weng Fanggang and Ruan Yuan; Yoo calls him a perfectionist who in youth drew charges of arrogance and who became more tolerant through his decade in exile, and notes the limits of his world view (in 1845 he dismissed the Samarang's appearance off Jeju and did not foresee the Qing collapse). Newspaper summary of one biographer's argument, with a critical voice.

Korea JoongAng Daily (Park Sung-ha), 'The small subtlety of calligraphy' (9 November 2005), report on the Gwacheon exhibition of 124 of his letters, poems, essays and paintings (read in full): the 1840 exile to Jeju after the Yun Sang-do memorial affair, the second exile to Bukcheong, the Bongeun Temple tablet said to be written three days before his death, a letter quoting his remark that after 70 years he had used up ten inkwells and over a thousand brushes, letters to the monk Choui asking for tea and letters to his wife; the exhibition curator says the letters matter for his life as a person, not only as an artist. Newspaper report on an exhibition, partly relying on his own letters.

Asia Business Daily (Ham Hyeri, cultural critic), 'The True Value of Sehando' (8 September 2020; read in full): after being exiled to Jeju in 1840, he painted Sehando in 1844 for his pupil Yi Sang-jeok, who had brought him rare books and inscriptions from Beijing; Yi showed it to Qing literati, sixteen of whom wrote colophons, producing a scroll over ten meters long; account of the painting's later owners, Fujitsuka Chikashi, Son Jae-hyung and the Son family, and its donation to the National Museum of Korea. Opinion column; reads the painting as a statement about loyalty.

The Korea Herald (Park Jeong-eon, senior researcher at the Chungnam Institute of History and Culture), 'Scholars and Their Spaces: Never despair. But if you do, work on in despair' (6 August 2022, via Daum; read in full): eight-plus years of confinement in a thorn-fenced house on Jeju, the Chusa style and Sehando completed in exile; more than 3,000 pupils from both the yangban and the technocrat classes, which was unusual in a hierarchical society; in youth he lacked tolerance, argued over right and wrong and cited original Chinese editions to ignore Joseon scholars; his view of life changed after exile; he always stressed that an artist must keep studying. Essay by a regional historian for a general readership.

The Korea Times (Kwon Mee-yoo), 'After Every Winter Comes Spring exhibition sheds light on ancestors' pursuit of hope' (24 November 2020; read in full): National Museum of Korea show built around Sehando (National Treasure No. 180) and the 15-meter scroll with Joseon and Qing colophons, shown with his letters to the friends and students who helped him in exile; notes the donation of the painting by Son Chang-geun and the later study of his art by O Se-chang, Son Jae-hyung and Fujitsuka Chikashi. News report on a museum exhibition.

persistence.rationale: [src_kim_encykorea, src_kim_herald, src_kim_joongang, src_kim_asiae | 1840-1856 | reference entry, regional-historian essay, newspaper reports] Four accounts agree that during roughly nine years of confinement on Jeju he kept reading and writing, produced Sehando in 1844 and the mature Chusa style there, and wrote a tablet for Bongeun Temple in the last days of his life. The accounts retell one adversity-into-art narrative rather than independent episodes, so the score stays in the 70s with moderate confidence.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_kim_encykorea, src_kim_kt2018, src_kim_geumseok | 1809-1850s | reference entries, newspaper summary of a biography] He took the Qing evidential scholarship of Weng Fanggang and Ruan Yuan and digested it through his own experience (the reference entry's reading of his essay on seeking truth from facts), argued against rigid Neo-Confucian debate (per his biographer), and in his orchid painting inscription wrote that his method would not be understood or liked by the public. The inscription is his own statement and the characterization of his originality comes from a small circle of experts.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_kim_encykorea, src_kim_kt2018, src_kim_joongang | 1830s-1850s | reference entry, newspaper reports] The reference entry describes the Chusa style as a personal script that broke popular taste and combined brush methods from the Tang-Song period to the Qing into something deliberately strange, which he himself called 'goe'; newspapers repeat that he created the style that bears his name. The judgment of originality rests on art-historical assessment and later reputation rather than independent behavioral episodes.

aesthetic_sensitivity.rationale: [src_kim_encykorea, src_kim_asiae | 1844 | reference entry, opinion column] In Sehando he stripped the scene to almost nothing and chose the title in Han clerical script, the inscription in early Wei-Jin regular script and the accompanying text in Northern Dynasties regular script, according to the reference entry; the column reads the dry brushwork as expressing his state in exile. Both accounts concern one work.

mastery_orientation.rationale: [src_kim_encykorea, src_kim_joongang, src_kim_herald | 1810s-1856 | reference entry, newspaper report quoting his letter, regional-historian essay] The reference entry records that he practiced classical scripts from the start (a surviving exercise copy of the Cao Quan stele at the Yesan house) and searched for over thirty years for the right character for the 'Chimgye' inscription; his letter, quoted by the exhibition report, says he had used up ten inkwells and over a thousand brushes in 70 years; the essay says he stressed continued study. The letter is his own statement and the thirty-year anecdote comes from his inscription.

curiosity.rationale: [src_kim_encykorea, src_kim_geumseok | 1810s-1830s | two entries from one encyclopedia] Two distinct lines of inquiry: he studied Western Han clerical script from bronze mirrors, lamps and brick inscriptions rather than only stele rubbings, and he investigated the Jinheung monuments, checking inscriptions against calendars and dynastic histories and sharing results with Chinese colleagues. Both entries are from the same encyclopedia, so independence is limited.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_kim_encykorea, src_kim_herald, src_kim_kt2018 | 1809-1856 | reference entry, regional-historian essay, newspaper summary] Work in epigraphy, classical studies, Buddhist thought (including debate with Seon masters), calligraphy, ink painting, seal carving, poetry and prose is described across three accounts; the biographer's remark that calligraphy was only one of his gifts matches the reference entry. Each area has some output, but the accounts describe breadth in summary form rather than a documented sequence of pivots.

belief_updating.rationale: [src_kim_geumseok, src_kim_herald, src_kim_kt2018 | 1817-1845 | reference entry, regional-historian essay, newspaper summary] His later study of the Jinheung monuments substantially revised the views of his earlier essay on them, and the essay says he changed after exile; against that, the biographer notes that in 1845 he dismissed the significance of the Western ship off Jeju and did not expect the Qing to fall. The evidence is mixed and pointed in different directions, so the score stays near the middle with low confidence.

perfectionism.rationale: [src_kim_kt2018, src_kim_encykorea | youth-1850s | newspaper summary, reference entry] His biographer calls him a perfectionist and links this to charges of arrogance in youth; the reference entry's 'Chimgye' story (over thirty years to find one character he had promised to write) is a single episode. One biographer's label and one episode support a modest lean.

detail_orientation.rationale: [src_kim_geumseok, src_kim_encykorea | 1817-1850s | two entries from one encyclopedia] The monument study checks the inscribed date against the Zhou calendar, assigns ranks and offices from the histories, and picks a spelling from a collector's record. All of this comes from one description of one work, and the reference entry's 'Chimgye' story is a second but related instance.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: [src_kim_herald, src_kim_encykorea | youth-1852 | regional-historian essay, reference entry] The essay says that in youth he argued over right and wrong in every case and cited original Chinese editions against Joseon scholars; the reference entry says he argued with Seon masters yet kept them as companions. These are general characterizations without a dated incident, and the youthful behavior is said to have softened after exile.

collaboration.rationale: [src_kim_encykorea, src_kim_herald, src_kim_joongang | 1810s-1850s | reference entry, regional-historian essay, newspaper report] He kept up scholarly exchange with Beijing colleagues and shared domestic monument research with them, took pupils across social classes and formed a circle of artists around him, and relied on friends and pupils (Choui, Yi Sang-jeok) in exile. The counts of pupils and the strength of ties are summaries, not documented joint projects.

discipline.rationale: [src_kim_joongang, src_kim_encykorea | 1810s-1856 | newspaper report quoting his letter, reference entry] His own letter about ten inkwells and a thousand brushes, practice copies of classical stele, and a tablet written three days before his death point to steady practice, but the first is a self-statement and the second and third are single items.

portrait.source: Gongyu Madang (Korea Copyright Commission), item 'Kim Jeong-hui chosang' (wrtSn 13365679), original file named 'Heo Ryeon, Kim Jeong-hui chosang, 19th century'; digital reproduction published by the Korea Data Agency (Kim Dal-jin Art Research Institute). The file is the portal's 1472 x 2065 image downscaled to 713 x 1000 with no upscaling. The original painting's present owner is not named by the portal.
portrait.license: Public domain by age: the portal labels the item 'free use, expired' (the author Heo Ryeon died in 1892; Korean protection is life plus 70 years). The 1920s colophons visible on the sheet are by Oh Se-chang (d. 1953, term expired after 2023) and Yun Hui-yeong (death date not established).
portrait.attribution: Heo Ryeon (Sochi, 1809-1892), copy of a portrait of Kim Jeong-hui, 19th century, with later colophons; via Gongyu Madang / Korea Data Agency. A copy by a pupil after an earlier portrait, not a documented sitting; not a lifetime likeness in the strict sense.
portrait.creator: Heo Ryeon (Sochi), pupil of the sitter
portrait.date: undated, 19th century (colophon dated to a gapja year, probably 1924)

provenance.notes: Roster70. portrait_preflight stageB PLAUSIBLE (lead: Yi Han-cheol 1857 official portrait via Commons PD scans). LEAD DID NOT SURVIVE: the item is a family-owned deposit at the National Museum of Korea, and the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture media record for the Yi Han-cheol portrait names the National Museum of Korea as copyright holder and states the image is not free to use or download outside the encyclopedia service, which overrides the Commons PD tag; no KOGL mark was found. REPLACEMENT: the Heo Ryeon depiction held on Gongyu Madang, item page read, labelled 'free use, expired' under the portal's own expired-works terms (read). The sheet carries the printed inscription 'Wandang Noseonsaeng sang' (portrait of the old master Wandang), 'Sochi Heo Ryeon sabon' (copy by Sochi Heo Ryeon), and later colophons by Oh Se-chang and Yun Hui-yeong, so sitter identity is established by lettering. KIND historical_depiction: a pupil's copy after an earlier portrait, undated, with a 1920s colophon. CAVEATS for lead review: Yun Hui-yeong's death year was not established (colophon rights), the portal does not name the owner of the original, and the portal's item page leaves its own 'source' and 'terms' fields blank in the text I could read (the license badge reads 'free use, expired'). HISTORICAL ATTRIBUTION: attributable (extensive writings, letters, dated works, court record), but most substantive evidence for traits comes from modern secondary reference and press, not contemporaries; sources actually read: Encyclopedia of Korean Culture main entry and the Geumseok gwaanrok entry, Korea Times 2018 and 2020, Korea JoongAng Daily 2005, Asia Business Daily 2020, Korea Herald 2022; Wikipedia raw text read for orientation only. Not opened: his collected works, the Wandang cheokdok letters, Fujitsuka Chikashi's study, Brother Anthony's Korean Tea Classics. POLITICS: the Yun Sang-do memorial affair and the Heonjong tomb dispute are context for the exiles and are not scored. LIMITS: only 13 rows are scored; no source describes assertiveness, risk-taking or decision-making with specific episodes; no padding. KO NAME: 김정희 is the Korean Wikipedia title, the Wikidata ko label and the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture headword. NOTE on fieldIds: art and literature are the closest existing ids; there is no id for epigraphy or history scholarship.
